name: Achan
title: The Man Who Took the Devoted Thing
summary: Achan, son of Karmi from the clan of Zerah in the tribe of Judah, became a warning figure in Israel's history when he took what was devoted to destruction (herem) from Jericho. Despite God's explicit command, he took a fine robe from Shinar, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels, and buried the loot under his tent. The violation brought immediate and dramatic consequences: God's presence and protection withdrew from the people, and Israel suffered an unexpected defeat against the small town of Ai, where thirty-six men fell. When Joshua threw himself down before the ark of the covenant in prayer, the Lord revealed that the camp had become unclean because someone had taken devoted things. A step-by-step process of casting lots – tribe, clan, household, individual – narrowed the search to Achan. Confronted face-to-face with his guilt, he made a frank confession describing the dynamics of desire: he saw, he coveted, he took. Then he was led to the Valley of Achor along with his family, possessions, and the stolen goods, and the whole assembly carried out the sentence by stoning and burning. The place received the name Achor – "Valley of Trouble" – as a lasting memorial. Achan's story shows that disobedience against God's holy commands affects more than just the guilty person, and that desire for what is forbidden can set off a chain of destruction for an entire people.

keyEvents.title: The Conquest of Jericho and Achan's Sin
keyEvents.description: After the fall of Jericho, Achan took some of the devoted things—a beautiful robe from Shinar, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels—and hid them under his tent, directly disobeying God's command that all devoted things must be destroyed or given to the Lord.

keyEvents.title: Israel's Defeat at Ai
keyEvents.description: Because of Achan's unfaithfulness, God turned away from Israel, and the people suffered an unexpected and humiliating defeat against the small town of Ai, where about 36 Israelites were killed and the rest put to flight.

keyEvents.title: Joshua's Prayer and God's Answer
keyEvents.description: After the defeat, Joshua fell on his face before the ark of the Lord's covenant and cried out to God in despair. The Lord revealed that Israel had sinned by taking some of the devoted things, and that the people would not be able to stand against their enemies until the sin was removed.

keyEvents.title: The Exposure of Achan
keyEvents.description: God commanded that Israel be presented tribe by tribe through casting lots. First the tribe of Judah was selected, then Zerah's clan, then Zimri's household, and finally Achan son of Karmi was revealed as the guilty one.

keyEvents.title: Achan's Confession
keyEvents.description: Joshua urged Achan to give glory to the Lord, the God of Israel, and make his confession. Achan admitted that he had seen, coveted, and taken a costly robe from Shinar, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels, and buried them in the ground under his tent.

keyEvents.title: The Judgment at the Valley of Achor
keyEvents.description: Achan was brought to the Valley of Achor along with the stolen goods, his sons and daughters, his livestock, and all he owned. All Israel stoned them, they were burned with fire, and covered with a large pile of stones. The place was named the Valley of Achor, meaning 'valley of trouble,' as a lasting witness to the consequences of breaking God's holy commands.

versions.summary: Achan was an Israelite from the tribe of Judah who sinned against God by taking some of the devoted things after the conquest of Jericho. His disobedience led to Israel's defeat at Ai and resulted in his own death by stoning in the Valley of Achor.
versions.title: The Man Who Stole from the Devoted Things
versions.reason: [minor] The amount of silver was according to Josh 7:21 two hundred shekels of silver and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels. The description does not mention the weight of the gold bar. It may be useful to include this for completeness.; [major] Achan's lineage goes through Zerah, but the text says 'the family of Zabdi'. In Josh 7:17-18 the order is: tribe of Judah → clan of Zerah → household of Zabdi → Achan. The correct Hebrew name is Zabdi (Achan's grandfather). It states 'the family of Zabdi' but it is actually the household of Carmi as the last link before Achan. The order should be: tribe of Judah → clan of Zerah → household of Zabdi → family of Carmi → Achan.; [minor] The text in Josh 7:24-25 also mentions that his sons, daughters, livestock and all he owned were brought with him to the Valley of Achor. That his family was involved is an important detail that should be mentioned, and it suggests that the 'children' field in family perhaps should reflect that he had children.; [major] According to Josh 7:24 Achan had sons and daughters who were brought with him to the Valley of Achor. The children field should not be empty, but since the names are unknown, this should at least be mentioned in the summary or a footnote.; [minor] Achan had sons and daughters according to Josh 7:24, which implies that he had a spouse, even though she is not named in the text.; [minor] 'Warrior' is reasonable, but Achan is primarily known as a warning example in biblical history. One might consider adding a role such as 'Israelite' to reflect his basic status.; [major] There are no footnotes with historical, archaeological, linguistic or theological details. The account of Achan has rich background that should be covered.

versions.summary: Achan was an Israelite from the tribe of Judah, son of Karmi, of the family of Zerah. After the conquest of Jericho, he broke God's command by taking some of the devoted things (herem) – a Babylonian robe, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels – and hid them under his tent. His disobedience caused God's anger to fall on all Israel, who suffered an unexpected defeat against the city of Ai. Through casting lots, Achan was exposed as the guilty one, and he confessed his sin to Joshua. He was then taken to the Valley of Achor ('Valley of Trouble') along with his family and everything he owned, and was stoned. Achan's story serves as a powerful warning about the consequences of disobedience and greed, and how one person's sin can affect the entire community.
versions.title: The Man Who Stole from the Devoted Things
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'The Man Who Stole from the Ban' is functional but could have been slightly more precise. The term 'stole' is somewhat colloquial—in a biblical context, he took from what was under the ban (herem). Nevertheless, the title is understandable and descriptive enough.; [minor] In the description of the revelation, 'Zabdi's household' is mentioned, but according to Joshua 7:17-18, it is Zabdi who is Akhan's grandfather (Karmi is his father). The Hebrew text states that Zabdi's household was taken man by man and Akhan was found. The name 'Zabdi' is used in some places, while 'Zibdi' appears elsewhere. Consider using the most consistent form, but this is a minor issue.; [minor] The role 'Israelite' is more an identity than a role. It could be considered to add 'sinner' or 'lawbreaker' as a role, but this might also be perceived as editorially loaded. Consider whether 'warrior' alone is sufficient.; [minor] The summary is good and theologically correct. It can be clarified that the cloak is described as a 'cloak from Shinar' (from Shinar/Babylonia) rather than simply 'Babylonian', to stay closer to the original text, but 'Babylonian' is an accepted rendering.; [minor] The description mentions 'a beautiful Babylonian cloak'—the original text uses 'aderet Shin'ar' (cloak from Shinar). 'Babylonian' is an interpretation, but it is accepted in most translations. Alternatively, 'from Shinar' could be mentioned for precision.

versions.summary: Achan, son of Karmi, was an Israelite from the clan of Zerah in the tribe of Judah. After the Israelites captured Jericho, he violated God's explicit command by taking some of the devoted things (herem) – a fine robe from Shinar, two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels – and hid them under his tent. This act provoked God's anger against all Israel, and the people suffered a shocking and humiliating defeat at the hands of the small town of Ai, where about 36 Israelites fell. When Joshua desperately sought the Lord's face, God revealed that someone in the camp had sinned by taking what was devoted. Through a casting of lots process, Achan was identified as the guilty one, and he made a full confession before Joshua and the people. He was then taken down to the Valley of Achor along with his family, his possessions, and the stolen goods, and all Israel carried out the sentence by stoning him. Achan's story is a powerful example of how greed and disobedience toward God's holy commands can have catastrophic consequences – not only for the individual, but for the entire community to which they belong.
versions.title: The Man Who Took the Devoted Thing
versions.reason: [minor] Achan had sons and daughters according to Josh 7:24, which implies that he had a spouse. Although the spouse is not mentioned by name, the spouse field could include a note about this. Likewise, the children array could reflect that he had children, even though they are not named. However, this is difficult to represent in the structure, so it is a minor issue.; [minor] The first footnote's transliteration of Achan as 'Akan' in parentheses is somewhat misleading. The Hebrew form עָכָן is normally transliterated as 'Akhan' or 'Akjan'. 'Akan' (עָכָן) is an acceptable variant, but the parentheses should be clearer.; [minor] The role 'Israelite' is more of an identity than a role. One might consider adding 'sinner' or 'violator of the herem commandment' to reflect his central function in the story, but the current roles are acceptable.

footnotes.text: The name Achan (Hebrew: עָכָן, 'Achan') is possibly related to the Hebrew verb עכר ('akar'), meaning 'to bring trouble.' In 1 Chr 2:7 he is called 'Akar,' which explicitly links his name to the trouble he brought upon Israel. This change of name may reflect a deliberate wordplay in the biblical text.

The Valley of Achor (Hebrew: עֵמֶק עָכוֹר) is also mentioned by the prophet Hosea (Hos 2:17), where it is transformed from a place of judgment into 'a door of hope.' This shows how a site associated with punishment in the book of Joshua gains a future redemptive meaning in prophetic literature.

The concept of 'herem' (חֵרֶם), the devoted thing, meant that everything in a conquered city was to be destroyed or dedicated to the Lord. This was common in Old Testament warfare and also known from other cultures in the ancient Near East, as documented on the Mesha Stele from Moab (ca. 840 BC).

Archaeological excavations at et-Tell, traditionally identified with Ai, have raised questions about the chronology of the conquest, since the site appears to have been uninhabited during parts of the Late Bronze Age. Alternative locations such as Khirbet el-Maqatir have been proposed by some scholars.

In rabbinic tradition (Sanhedrin 44a), Achan's sin is discussed as an example of how one person's actions can affect the entire community. The Talmud also debates whether his confession secured him a place in the world to come.

The Hebrew phrase for 'a beautiful robe from Shinar' (אַדֶּרֶת שִׁנְעָר) refers to a luxurious garment from the region of Shinar (Babylonia). Such robes were prized trade goods in the ancient Near East and testify to trade routes between Mesopotamia and Canaan already in the Bronze Age.

The punishment of Achan and his family raises difficult theological questions about collective guilt. In ancient Israel, the family and household were seen as a unit, and one person's unfaithfulness could defile the entire group. This concept of collective responsibility was widespread in the ancient Near East and must be understood within its cultural context.

The casting of lots used to identify Achan (Josh 7:14–18) is an example of using sacred lots (possibly Urim and Thummim) to determine God's will. This practice is well attested in the Old Testament and served as a means of divine revelation in important decisions.
